newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: YEAREND-Ringgit seen boosted by high interest rates.
newsitem.headline: YEAREND-Ringgit seen boosted by high interest rates.

text.p: The Malaysian ringgit is expected to benefit from improving economic fundamentals and high domestic interest rates in 1997, but a shift in U.S. monetary policy may affect the trend, analysts said on Tuesday.
While the ringgit may not move out of its current range against the U.S. dollar in the near term, it was expected to begin gaining from the end of the second quarter, they said.
"The ringgit should have a good next year," said Jimmy Koh, economist with research firm I.D.E.A. in Singapore.

"The government has reaffirmed its tight monetary policy, which means high interest rates will stay at least till the third quarter of 1997. The current account deficit is down sharply and is expected to fall further," he said.

In addition, the ringgit and the Indonesian rupiah would be the main beneficiaries of this year's traditional Japanese fund outflows to high-yielding currencies around April, the Thai baht having lost out due to political and other domestic factors.
"We could see the ringgit breaking 2.4775/85 (a dollar) high seen this year," Koh said.
In a poll by Reuters, 16 research houses forecast in late November that the ringgit is expected to gain to an average 2.4938 a dollar by the end of 1997.

The ringgit is expected to end the last day of the year around 2.5275/85 a dollar against 2.5385 at the end of 1995. It hit a low of 2.5680 a dollar on January 17 before setting on a recovery course that lasted most of the year.
The two main factors that triggered the recovery of the ringgit were an improvement in the country's trade balance and a slowdown in the fast-paced economic growth.

Malaysia is expected to end 1996 with a gross domestic product growth of 8.2 percent after 9.5 percent in 1995. The country has reported nine straight years of over eight percent growth, which is expected to be maintained till the year 2000.

Malaysia has recorded a sharply lower trade deficit of 954.35 million ringgit ($378.7 million) in the first 10 months of 1996 against around 9.96 billion ringgit in the corresponding period of last year.
The country's growing current account deficit and inflation had triggered worries about overheating and forced it to maintain a high interest rate regime to slow down growth.

However, the forecast trend may be derailed if there are changes in U.S. interest rates. In a recent speech, U.S. Federal Reserve Board Chairman Alan Greenspan was said to have hinted at a possible increase in interest rates.
The board's policy making body, the Federal Open Market Committee's (FOMC) meeting in February is keenly awaited by the market, dealers in Malaysia and Singapore said.
"Until then ringgit may track dollar's moves against other major currencies," the head of dealing at a Malaysian bank said, adding, "At the moment, dollar undertone is very bullish."
He said the ringgit would move between 2.50 and 2.55 a dollar in the first quarter.
Another Malaysian bank dealer said the ringgit would trade between 2.5180 and 2.5310 a dollar in the first month of 1997, possibly heading to 2.54 in February.
